¿Cómo se sabe si una serie converge?: How do you know whether a series converges?
Primero la condición necesaria: si aₙ no: First the necessary condition: if aₙ does not tend to 0, it diverges. Then try the ratio test (L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|: converges if L < 1, diverges if L > 1), the root test or comparison with 1/nᵖ, which converges if p > 1. For example, Σ 2ⁿ/n! has L = lim 2/(n + 1) = 0 and converges; its sum from n = 0 is e² ≈ 7.389.
¿Qué diferencia hay entre convergencia a: What is the difference between absolute and conditional convergence?
Converge absolutamente si Σ|aₙ| converge: It converges absolutely if Σ|aₙ| converges, and conditionally if Σaₙ converges but Σ|aₙ| does not. Σ(−1)ⁿ/n² converges absolutely (sum −π²/12), while Σ(−1)ⁿ/n converges only conditionally by the Leibniz test (sum −ln 2).

Sumas parciales de la serie y su suma: Partial sums of the series and its sum
Una serie $∑ a_n$ converge si las sumas: A series $∑ a_n$ converges if the partial sums $S_N = a_{n_0} + … + a_N$ approach a number $S$ as $N → ∞$; if not, it diverges. If $∑ |a_n|$ converges, the series converges absolutely; if $∑ a_n$ converges but $∑ |a_n|$ does not, it converges conditionally.
<b>Condición necesaria:</b> si $a_n \\no: Necessary condition: if $a_n \not→ 0$, the series diverges. If $a_n → 0$ nothing is known (the harmonic series $∑ 1/n$ diverges).
<b>Geométrica</b> $∑ r^n$: converge si $: Geometric $∑ r^n$: converges if $|r| < 1$ and its sum is $a_{n_0}/(1 − r)$.
<b>Serie p</b> $∑ 1/n^p$: converge si y: p-series $∑ 1/n^p$: converges if and only if $p > 1$. If $a_n ≈ C/n^p$ for large $n$, it is compared with it (limit comparison).
<b>Cociente:</b> $L = lím |a_{n+1}/a_n|$: Ratio: $L = lim |a_{n+1}/a_n|$. It converges absolutely if $L < 1$, diverges if $L > 1$ and is inconclusive if $L = 1$.
<b>Leibniz:</b> si los signos se alterna: Leibniz: if the signs alternate, $|a_n|$ decreases and $a_n → 0$, the series converges, and the error of stopping at $S_N$ is less than $|a_{N+1}|$.
Si $a_n = f(n)$ con $f$ positiva y decre: If $a_n = f(n)$ with $f$ positive and decreasing from some $m$ on, the series $∑ a_n$ and the improper integral $∫_m^∞ f(x) dx$ either both converge or both diverge. It is the test that decides when the ratio and root tests give 1 and logarithms appear: $∑ 1/(n \ ln n)$ diverges because its antiderivative $ln(ln x)$ grows without bound, and $∑ 1/(n \ ln^2 n)$ converges because its own, $−1/ln x$, tends to 0. The tool looks for the antiderivative and computes the limit; if there is no elementary antiderivative, it estimates the integral numerically and says so.
Esa desigualdad también encierra el rest: That inequality also bounds the remainder of the series, and with it the sum is given for series that converge so slowly that adding terms is not enough.
